Caleb's kin; routs Cushan-Rishathaim of Aram. The land rests 40 years.

300 men with trumpets and torches scatter Midian. The land rests 40 years.

Bears God's covenant with David's house, then confronts him over Bathsheba: 'Thou art the man.'
Solomon's son; his harsh word at Shechem tears ten tribes away. Reigns 17 years.

A good king who tears down idols and is healed of none of his foot disease. Reigns 41 years.
Godly and reforming, but yokes himself to Ahab's house by marriage. Reigns 25 years.
Marries Athaliah of Ahab's line and walks in Israel's ways. Reigns 8 years.
Grandson of Ahab through his mother Athaliah; killed by Jehu in the great purge after one year.
Ahab's daughter murders the royal seed and seizes the throne 6 years — the one break in David's line.
Hidden as an infant by his aunt Jehosheba, crowned at seven by Jehoiada the priest; repairs the Temple, then falls after the priest dies. 40 years.
Defeats Edom, then provokes Israel and is beaten at Beth-shemesh. Reigns 29 years.
A long, strong reign undone when he burns incense unlawfully and is struck with leprosy. 52 years.
Builds and grows mighty because he orders his ways before the LORD. Reigns 16 years.
Sacrifices his son and strips the Temple to buy Assyria's help; Isaiah gives him the Immanuel sign. 16 years.
Cleanses the Temple, defies Assyria and is given 15 added years. Reigns 29 years.
Judah's longest and most wicked reign — 55 years — yet he repents in a Babylonian prison.
Returns to his father's idols; his own servants kill him after 2 years.
The great reformer; the Book of the Law is found in his 18th year. Reigns 31 years, then falls at Megiddo.
Reigns 3 months before Pharaoh Necho carries him to Egypt.
Necho's puppet who burns Jeremiah's scroll; Babylon makes him a vassal. Reigns 11 years.
Reigns 3 months, then is carried to Babylon with the craftsmen and treasures (the first great deportation).
The last king; rebels against Babylon and watches his sons die before his eyes are put out. 11 years to the fall.
First king of the north; sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan 'lest the people go up to Jerusalem.' 22 years.
Jeroboam's son; struck down by Baasha, ending the first dynasty. 2 years.
Wipes out Jeroboam's house and reigns 24 years in the same sins.
Baasha's son; murdered drunk by his chariot captain Zimri. 2 years.
Reigns 7 days, then burns the palace over himself when Omri closes in.
Founds Samaria as capital and a lasting dynasty; 'did worse than all before him.' 12 years.
Marries Jezebel and enthrones Baal; the great foil of Elijah. 22 years.
Falls through a lattice and sends to Baal-zebub instead of God; dies as Elijah foretold. 2 years.
Ahab's son; slain by Jehu at Naboth's field, ending the house of Omri. 12 years.
Jehu's son; Israel ground down to almost nothing under Aram. 17 years.
Weeps over dying Elisha and wins three victories over Aram. 16 years.
Restores Israel's borders in a long, prosperous, and idolatrous reign — the age of Amos and Hosea. 41 years.
Jehu's line ends in the fourth generation exactly as promised (2 Kings 10:30); after the anarchy that follows Jeroboam II he is slain within six months.
Reigns one month before Menahem cuts him down.
Buys off Assyria's Pul with silver wrung from the land. 10 years.
Menahem's son; killed by his officer Pekah. 2 years.
Allies with Aram against Judah in the Syro-Ephraimite war; loses Galilee and Gilead to Assyria. His 20 years (2 Kings 15:27) overlap the last northern kings before Hoshea conspires and kills him.
The last northern king; his revolt brings Shalmaneser, and after 9 years Samaria falls.
Tears his cloak in twelve pieces to foretell the split, then dooms Jeroboam's house.
Halts Rehoboam's war on the north — 'this thing is from Me' — and later reads Judah Shishak's judgment.
Shuts up heaven three years, calls fire on Carmel, and is taken up in a whirlwind. The great foe of Baal.
Alone against 450 prophets of Baal, he calls down fire and turns the people back: 'The LORD, He is God.'
Alone foretells Ahab's death at Ramoth-gilead against 400 flattering prophets.
Takes up Elijah's mantle and a double portion; heals, raises the dead, and topples kings for 50 years.
The shortest book: Edom is doomed for gloating over fallen Jacob.
Reads a locust plague as the Day of the LORD and foretells the Spirit poured out on all flesh.
Flees his call, is swallowed and spared, then watches Nineveh repent to his dismay.
A herdsman sent north 'two years before the earthquake' to thunder against Israel's ease and injustice.
Marries the unfaithful Gomer as a living parable of the LORD's love for wayward Israel.
Sees the LORD high and lifted up in Uzziah's death-year; prophet of the Holy One and the coming Servant.
Names Bethlehem as the ruler's birthplace and asks only to do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly.
Generations after Jonah spared Nineveh, he pronounces its ruin: the LORD is slow to anger but will not acquit the guilty.
Kinsman of the kings; heralds the Day of the LORD in Josiah's reign and calls Judah to seek meekness.
Called in Josiah's 13th year as 'a prophet to the nations'; weeps over Judah for forty years to the fall.
Wrestles with why God would use Babylon, and is answered: 'the just shall live by his faith.'

event: Jeroboam's golden calves at Bethel & Dan
notes: The north's founding sin: two calves 'lest the people go up to Jerusalem,' a snare to Israel for good.
Anointed to wipe out Baal and the house of Ahab; the LORD grants his line four generations. Reigns 28 years.

event: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath
notes: Through the famine her jar of meal and cruse of oil never fail, and her dead son is raised — mercy to a Gentile in Baal's own country.
Jezebel has Naboth stoned so Ahab can take his vineyard; Elijah pronounces the doom that Jehu will one day execute on this very ground.

event: Elijah taken up in a whirlwind
notes: Fire and horses part the two prophets; Elijah ascends, and Elisha takes up the fallen mantle with a double portion.

event: Naaman the Syrian healed by Elisha
notes: The Aramean commander dips seven times in the Jordan and his leprosy is gone — a sign the God of Israel is God of all.

event: The great earthquake in Uzziah's days
notes: So violent it is remembered for centuries; Amos dates his oracles 'two years' before it.

event: Isaiah gives Ahaz the Immanuel sign
notes: As Aram and Israel besiege Jerusalem, Isaiah promises the faithless king a sign: a virgin shall conceive and bear Immanuel.
He reopens the cleansed Temple and summons all Israel — even the north — to a Passover unmatched since Solomon.
Sick unto death, he turns his face to the wall and weeps; God adds fifteen years and turns the shadow back on the dial.

event: Hezekiah's tunnel to the Siloam pool
notes: Ahead of the siege he cuts an aqueduct through solid rock to bring the Gihon spring inside the walls.
Judah's worst king is dragged to Babylon with hooks; there he humbles himself, and God restores him — the sharpest picture of grace in the monarchy.

event: Huldah the prophetess authenticates the Law
notes: When the lost scroll is found, Josiah's men go to Huldah; she confirms the coming judgment but promises the king will die in peace.
No Passover like it had been kept since the days of the judges — the high point of the last reformation before the fall.
Column by column the king slices the prophet's warnings into the brazier — so Jeremiah dictates them again, with more added.
A shepherd boy with a sling fells the Philistine champion in the Valley of Elah, and Israel's deliverer steps onto the stage.

event: Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz
notes: 'In the days when the judges ruled,' a Moabite widow's loyalty grafts her into Israel — and into the line of David and the Messiah.
A Jerusalem sage's book of wisdom; his grandson's Greek preface (132 BC) is one of the few fixed dates in the silent years.
Josephus first names the three 'schools' of the Jews — the very parties that will fill the pages of the Gospels.
A priestly community withdraws to the Dead Sea to keep the Law and await the LORD; their hidden library surfaces in 1947.
Hyrcanus subdues Edom and compels the Idumeans to be circumcised as Jews — a century later one of them, Herod, will rule as 'King of the Jews.'
The Maccabean high priests now claim the crown as well — priest and king in one house, against the Law's own separation.

event: Alexander Jannaeus rules; Judea at its height
notes: The Hasmonean kingdom reaches its widest borders under a warrior-priest whose cruelty turns the Pharisees against the dynasty.

event: Queen Salome Alexandra reigns in peace
notes: The one Hasmonean queen; she makes peace with the Pharisees — Judea's last calm before Rome.

event: Civil war: Hyrcanus II vs Aristobulus II
notes: The brothers' quarrel over throne and altar draws Pompey's Rome into Judea — the fatal invitation.
On his way to the Parthians who will kill him, the Roman triumvir strips 2,000 talents from the house of God.

event: Antigonus, last Hasmonean king; Parthians take Jerusalem
notes: The Parthians install the last Maccabee on the throne; Herod flees to Rome — and returns with legions and a crown.

event: David anointed by Samuel at Bethlehem
notes: The youngest son, keeping sheep, is anointed in secret — the LORD looks not on the outward appearance but on the heart.

event: Death of Saul and Jonathan at Gilboa
notes: Israel's first king falls on his own sword as the Philistines overrun Mount Gilboa; David laments, 'How are the mighty fallen.'

event: David brings the Ark to Jerusalem
notes: Uzzah dies steadying it, and then it comes up with shouting and trumpets as David dances before the LORD with all his might.
David would build God a house; instead God vows to build David a house — a throne and a Son whose kingdom shall have no end.
The king takes Uriah's wife and hides murder under adultery; Nathan's parable springs the trap — 'Thou art the man.'
David's own son steals the people's hearts and drives him from Jerusalem; the revolt ends with Absalom caught in an oak and a father weeping, 'O Absalom, my son.'

event: David numbers Israel; Araunah's threshing floor
notes: His census brings a plague; where the destroying angel stays his hand, on Araunah's floor, Solomon will one day raise the Temple.

event: Solomon asks for wisdom at Gibeon
notes: Offered anything, the young king asks not for wealth or long life but for a discerning heart — and is given all three.

event: The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon
notes: She comes to test him with hard questions and leaves overwhelmed: the half of his wisdom and glory had not been told her.

event: Solomon's foreign wives turn his heart to idolatry
notes: A thousand wives and concubines draw the wisest man alive into idolatry; for this the LORD will tear ten tribes from his son.
On the Gaza road he baptizes a court official of Ethiopia — the gospel already running toward the ends of the earth.

event: Peter and Cornelius; the gospel opens to the Gentiles
notes: The Spirit falls on a Roman centurion's household still uncircumcised; Peter concludes that God shows no partiality.
In the great mixed church of Antioch the movement is first given the name it will carry ever after.

event: Paul's second journey; the gospel enters Europe
notes: A vision of a man of Macedonia draws Paul across the Aegean to Philippi — the gospel steps onto European soil.
From Corinth he sends the church's earliest surviving letters, steadying young believers on the return of the Lord.
On the eve of his last journey to Jerusalem he sets out the gospel in full to a church he has never seen.
Fourteen storm-tossed nights end on Malta; unharmed by a viper, the prisoner reaches Rome at last.

event: The Synoptic Gospels take written form
notes: Within a generation of the resurrection the eyewitness accounts are set down for the churches.

notes: The golden lampstand and table are paraded through Rome — and carved forever onto the Arch of Titus.

section: FALL OF JERUSALEM & THE APOSTLE JOHN
notes: The emperor who demands to be hailed 'Lord and God' turns on the church — the fire behind John's Revelation.

section: FALL OF JERUSALEM & THE APOSTLE JOHN
event: Clement of Rome writes to Corinth
notes: The earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament, already pleading for order in a divided church.

source: Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), rediscovered 1873
notes: Somewhere in Syria the young church wrote down its first manual, mapping the Two Ways of life and death and how to baptize and break bread.

source: Ignatius, Seven Epistles; Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. 3.36
notes: Dragged in chains from Antioch to Rome, the old bishop wrote seven letters urging unity under the bishop and longed to be 'God's wheat' ground by the lions.

From his post in Bithynia a puzzled Roman governor asked the emperor how to try these Christians who met at dawn to sing 'to Christ as to a god,' and Trajan told him not to hunt them but to punish the accused.

source: Tertullian, Against Marcion; Irenaeus, Against Heresies
notes: Expelled by the church of Rome, Marcion severed the God of the Old Testament from the Father of Jesus and published a slimmed-down Luke and ten letters of Paul, forcing the church to name its own Scriptures in reply.

source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies; the Nag Hammadi library
notes: In the salons of Rome and Alexandria, Gnostic teachers like Valentinus peddled secret knowledge and a lesser Creator-god, the great rival the fathers would spend a century refuting.

source: The Martyrdom of Polycarp; Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. 4.15
notes: In the arena at Smyrna the aged bishop, a disciple of the Apostle John, refused to curse Christ: 'Eighty-six years I have served Him, and He has done me no wrong.'

source: Justin, First & Second Apology, Dialogue with Trypho; Acts of Justin
notes: Still wearing his philosopher's cloak, Justin argued in Rome that Christ was the Logos glimpsed by Socrates, then sealed his defense with his blood under the prefect Rusticus.

In the villages of Phrygia, Montanus and the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla claimed fresh outpourings of the Spirit and an imminent end, a rigorist enthusiasm that would one day win over Tertullian himself.
This battered Latin list, likely from Rome, is the earliest surviving catalogue of accepted New Testament books, showing the canon visibly taking shape.

source: Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. 5.1 (Letter of the Churches of Lyons and Vienne)
notes: Under Marcus Aurelius the mob of Gaul turned on the church, and the frail slave girl Blandina and the ninety-year-old bishop Pothinus outlasted the amphitheater's cruelty until the crowds themselves fell silent.

source: Athenagoras of Athens, Legatio pro Christianis
notes: An Athenian philosopher addressed Marcus Aurelius with calm reason, dismantling the rumors of atheism, cannibalism, and incest whispered against believers.
The bishop of Lyons, who as a boy had heard Polycarp, demolished the Gnostic myths and anchored the faith in the fourfold Gospel and the line of bishops reaching back to the apostles.

source: Tertullian, Against the Jews 7; Bede; the tradition of Alban
notes: Tertullian could already boast that corners of Britain unconquered by the legions had bowed to Christ, and at Verulamium the soldier Alban became the island's first martyr.

source: Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. 1.13; Doctrine of Addai; Bardaisan
notes: Beyond Rome's eastern frontier the gospel took root at Edessa in Mesopotamia and grew up speaking Syriac, giving the East its own scholars, hymns, and the legend of King Abgar.
The fierce North African lawyer wrote theology in Latin for the first time, coined the word 'Trinity,' and demanded to know what Athens had to do with Jerusalem.
Head of Alexandria's famous catechetical school, he wooed Greek philosophy into the service of Christ before fleeing the Severan storm.

event: Perpetua, Felicity and the Severan Persecution
source: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity; edict of Septimius Severus
notes: At Carthage a young nursing mother and her pregnant slave went to the beasts together, Perpetua's own prison diary preserving a woman's unbroken faith after Severus forbade conversion.

source: Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies; Tertullian, Against Praxeas
notes: At Rome Sabellius taught that Father, Son, and Spirit were merely three masks of one solitary God, a tidy monotheism the church rejected for erasing the persons it confessed.

source: Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. 6; Origen, On First Principles, Hexapla
notes: The tireless Alexandrian scholar built the six-column Hexapla and the first systematic theology, convinced that every line of Scripture, rightly read, spoke of Christ.

source: Cyprian, On the Lapsed; Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. 6.39; surviving libelli
notes: Emperor Decius ordered every subject to sacrifice to the gods and carry a certificate, the first empire-wide persecution, which yielded both bold martyrs and a flood of the 'lapsed.'

source: Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. 7.10-11; Acts of Cyprian
notes: Valerian struck at the leaders and the rich, and among the slain were Pope Sixtus II and the deacon Lawrence of Rome, remembered for jesting on his gridiron, 'Turn me over, I am done on this side.'

source: Cyprian, Epistles, On the Unity of the Church; Pontius, Life of Cyprian
notes: The bishop who steered Carthage through the agony of the lapsed and declared 'no salvation outside the Church' was beheaded under Valerian, calming his own executioner.

event: Antony of Egypt Enters the Desert
notes: A young Coptic farmer heard the gospel read, sold all he had, and withdrew into the Egyptian wilderness, kindling the monastic movement that would spread from the Nile across all Christendom.
When Gregory the Illuminator converted King Tiridates III, Armenia became the first nation on earth to embrace Christianity as its state faith, a full decade before Rome relented.

source: Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. 8; Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors
notes: The last and fiercest imperial assault razed churches, burned Scriptures, and jailed clergy across the empire, yet the blood of the martyrs proved, as Tertullian had said, the seed of the Church.

source: Rufinus, Hist. Eccl. 1.9-10; Athanasius, Apology to Constantius 31
notes: Shipwrecked as a boy on the Red Sea coast, Frumentius rose to serve the Aksumite court and won King Ezana to Christ, planting the Ethiopian church that endures to this day.

source: Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors 34; Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. 8.17
notes: Dying in agony at Serdica, Galerius confessed defeat and grudgingly legalized the faith he had tried to crush, ending the Great Persecution two years before Constantine's edict at Milan.

source: Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 44; Eusebius, Life of Constantine I.28
notes: At the Tiber's edge north of Rome, Constantine marks his soldiers' shields with Christ's monogram, routs Maxentius, and 'in this sign' turns the empire's fortune toward the faith.

source: Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 48; Eusebius, Eccl. Hist. X.5
notes: From Milan, Constantine and Licinius end three centuries of persecution, granting Christians the freedom to worship and restoring their confiscated churches across the Roman world.

event: First Council of Nicaea & the Homoousion
source: Athanasius, De Decretis; Eusebius; Socrates Scholasticus, Eccl. Hist. I
notes: Summoned by Constantine to a lakeside palace in Bithynia, some 300 bishops adopt the non-biblical term homoousios ('one in being') for the Son and condemn Arius. The word was resisted as unclear; Constantine pressed it through, and all but two bishops signed under his patronage and pressure.

event: Frumentius Carries the Faith to Ethiopia
source: Rufinus, Eccl. Hist. I.9; Athanasius, Apologia ad Constantium 31
notes: A shipwrecked youth turned royal tutor at Axum, Frumentius is consecrated by Athanasius and returns to plant the Church that endures in Ethiopia to this day.

source: Sozomen, Eccl. Hist. II.3; Zosimus, Historia Nova II
notes: On the Bosphorus, Constantine dedicates 'New Rome' — Constantinople — the Christian capital that will anchor the Eastern Church for a thousand years.
Baptized only on his deathbed near Nicomedia, the first Christian emperor dies, leaving both an empire and a Church he had forever transformed.

source: Philostorgius, Eccl. Hist. II.5; Auxentius of Durostorum
notes: Beyond the Danube among the Goths, the missionary Ulfilas invents an alphabet and renders Scripture into Gothic — the first Bible in any Germanic tongue.

At the dedication of Constantine's Golden Church in Antioch, Eastern bishops issue creeds that avoid Nicaea's homoousios — beginning two decades in which non-Nicene positions, not Nicaea, most often led the way.

source: Athanasius, Apologia contra Arianos 36-50; Socrates, Eccl. Hist. II.20
notes: Called to Sardica to reconcile East and West, the bishops instead walk out on one another — an early fault line running between Greek and Latin Christendom.

source: Athanasius, Apologia de Fuga; Socrates, Eccl. Hist. II; Sozomen IV
notes: As soldiers storm his basilica in Alexandria, Athanasius flees to the desert monks — 'Athanasius against the world' — enduring five exiles rather than surrender the Nicene faith.

source: Hilary of Poitiers, De Synodis 11; Athanasius, De Synodis 28
notes: The council later branded the 'Blasphemy of Sirmium' bars the word homoousios and urges the churches to drop 'substance' language about God altogether.

source: Jerome, Dialogue against the Luciferians 19; Athanasius, De Synodis
notes: At twin councils in West and East, imperial pressure yields a compromise creed preferring 'like' to 'same substance' — prompting Jerome's later lament that 'the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.'

source: Basil, Letters & On the Holy Spirit; Gregory Nazianzen, Theological Orations; Gregory of Nyssa
notes: From Caesarea, Basil the Great and the two Gregories refine the vocabulary — one 'being' (ousia) in three 'persons' (hypostases) — easing the confusion by philosophy rather than by Scripture. Their formula would prevail, though settled less by persuasion than by the emperor who came next.
From Thessalonica, Theodosius commands all his subjects to hold the Nicene faith, makes it the religion of the Roman state, and brands dissenters 'heretics' liable to civil penalty.

source: Socrates, Eccl. Hist. V.8; the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed; canons of 381
notes: Convened by Theodosius the year after he outlawed dissent, 150 bishops finalize the Creed and affirm the Spirit's divinity — the Nicene settlement now carried by imperial law as much as by agreement.

event: Ambrose of Milan Humbles an Emperor
source: Ambrose, Epistle 51; Theodoret, Eccl. Hist. V.17-18; Paulinus, Life of Ambrose
notes: In Milan, Bishop Ambrose bars the church doors to Theodosius after a massacre at Thessalonica, forcing the master of the world to kneel in public penance.

event: Permanent Division of East and West
source: Zosimus, Historia Nova V; Orosius, Historiae VII
notes: When Theodosius dies, the empire passes to his young sons — Arcadius in the East, Honorius in the West — and Rome is sundered into two halves that never reunite.
From his study in Hippo, Augustine pours out his restless heart to God — 'our hearts are restless until they rest in Thee' — in the West's first great spiritual autobiography.

source: Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom; Socrates, Eccl. Hist. VI
notes: The golden-mouthed preacher of Antioch is made archbishop of Constantinople, where his fearless sermons against luxury and vice earn him exile and death on the road.

source: Jerome, Prefaces to the Vulgate; Epistulae
notes: In a cave beside the Nativity grotto in Bethlehem, Jerome finishes translating the Scriptures into Latin from the original tongues — the Vulgate that Europe will read for a thousand years.

source: Jerome, Epistle 127; Orosius, Historiae VII.39; Augustine, City of God I
notes: For the first time in 800 years a foreign army — Alaric's Visigoths — breaches the Eternal City, and a shaken empire wonders whether the old gods have taken their revenge.

source: Augustine, anti-Donatist works; Optatus, Against the Donatists; Gesta Collationis Carthaginiensis
notes: At the Conference of Carthage the rigorist Donatists — who denied that fallen clergy could give valid sacraments — are ruled against, though their North African rift festers on for a century.
Answering pagans who blamed Rome's fall on Christ, Augustine writes City of God, setting the fleeting City of Man against the eternal City of God.

source: Council of Carthage (418); Pope Zosimus, Epistola Tractoria; Augustine, De gratia Christi
notes: At Carthage the Church condemns Pelagius' teaching that people can be sinless by their own effort, siding with Augustine's insistence on the priority of grace.
As Vandal armies besiege the walls of his own city of Hippo, the greatest theologian of the Latin West dies, closing the golden age of the Church Fathers.

source: Acta of Ephesus; Cyril of Alexandria, Letters; Socrates, Eccl. Hist. VII
notes: In the Church of Mary at Ephesus, Cyril of Alexandria and the council depose Nestorius and declare the Virgin Theotokos, 'God-bearer.'

event: Nestorian Departure & the Church of the East
source: Barhadbeshabba; School of Nisibis records; later Synod of Beth Lapat (484)
notes: Refusing Ephesus, Nestorius' followers carry their faith east into Persia, birthing the Church of the East that would one day reach India and China.

source: Patrick, Confessio; Muirchú, Life of Patrick; Bede, Eccl. Hist. (with Ninian, HE III.4)
notes: Once a slave in Ireland, Patrick returns as a missionary bishop to the very people who had seized him, kindling — with Ninian among the Picts — a Celtic Christianity that would help re-evangelize Europe.

event: Council of Chalcedon & the Two Natures
source: Acta of Chalcedon; Leo the Great, Tome (Ep. 28); Chalcedonian Definition
notes: Before some 500 bishops, Pope Leo's Tome prevails and the council defines Christ as one person in two natures — a formula the Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches will refuse.

event: The Oriental Orthodox Depart After Chalcedon
source: Zachariah Rhetor; Evagrius Scholasticus, Eccl. Hist.; Coptic & Syriac traditions
notes: Rejecting Chalcedon's 'two natures,' the Coptic, Syriac, and Armenian churches go their own way as the Oriental Orthodox — great communions permanently sundered from the imperial Church of Byzantium.

event: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
source: Jordanes, Getica 46; Anonymus Valesianus; Marcellinus Comes, Chronicle
notes: At Ravenna the boy-emperor Romulus Augustulus is deposed by the Germanic general Odoacer, who ships the imperial regalia to Constantinople, and the Roman West quietly comes to its end.

source: Leo I, Tome to Flavian (Ep. 28); Acts of the Council of Chalcedon (451)
notes: From Rome, Pope Leo I sends his Tome to Chalcedon, where the bishops cry 'Peter has spoken through Leo,' cementing both the two natures of Christ and Rome's claim to primacy.

source: Procopius, History of the Wars; The Secret History
notes: Ascending the throne in Constantinople, Justinian dreams of restoring the whole Roman world under one emperor, one law, and one orthodox faith.

source: Corpus Juris Civilis (Codex Justinianus, revised 534; Digest 533); Tribonian's commission
notes: In Constantinople Justinian's jurists distill centuries of Roman law into Code, Digest, and Institutes, the legal bedrock of Christendom for a thousand years.

source: Procopius, Buildings (De Aedificiis) I.1; Paul the Silentiary, Descriptio
notes: Dedicating his vast domed church in Constantinople, Justinian is said to exclaim 'Solomon, I have surpassed thee,' raising the crowning glory of Byzantine Orthodoxy.

source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues Book II; Regula Benedicti (Rule of St. Benedict)
notes: At Monte Cassino south of Rome, Benedict founds his monastery and writes a Rule of prayer and work ('ora et labora') that will shape all Western monasticism.

source: Acts of the Second Council of Constantinople (553), the Fifth Ecumenical Council
notes: The Fifth Ecumenical Council meets in Constantinople to condemn the 'Three Chapters,' straining to win back the eastern churches divided since Chalcedon.

source: Adomnan, Vita Columbae (Life of St. Columba); Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.4
notes: Sailing from Ireland, Columba founds a monastery on the tiny isle of Iona, a beacon from which Celtic monks will evangelize the Picts of Scotland and northern Britain.

source: Gregory the Great, Register of Letters; John the Deacon, Vita Gregorii; Bede, Eccl. History II
notes: A monk reluctantly made pope, Gregory I feeds Rome's poor, reforms its worship, and sends missionaries abroad, becoming the true founder of the medieval papacy.

source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People I.25-26
notes: Sent by Gregory the Great, Augustine lands in Kent and baptizes King Ethelbert, planting the Roman church among the Anglo-Saxons at Canterbury.

source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah; al-Tabari, History of the Prophets and Kings
notes: Muhammad flees Mecca for Medina; this Hijra begins the Muslim calendar and launches the movement that will soon sweep the ancient Christian heartlands.

source: al-Tabari, History; Theophanes the Confessor, Chronographia
notes: Caliph Umar enters Jerusalem as Patriarch Sophronius surrenders the holy city, and the birthplace of the church passes under Islamic rule.

source: John of Nikiu, Chronicle; al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan
notes: Amr ibn al-As takes Alexandria, ancient seat of Athanasius and Cyril, severing one of Christianity's greatest patriarchates from Byzantium.

event: The Fall of Christian North Africa
source: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr wa'l-Maghrib; Theophanes, Chronographia
notes: With the fall of Carthage the Umayyads sweep away the church of Tertullian, Cyprian, and Augustine of Hippo, extinguishing the Latin Christianity of the North African coast where so much of it was born.

source: Acts of the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681), the Sixth Ecumenical Council
notes: The Sixth Ecumenical Council condemns Monothelitism and confesses that Christ has two wills, human and divine, moving in perfect harmony.

source: Chronicle of 754 (Mozarabic Chronicle); al-Maqqari, Nafh al-Tib
notes: Tariq ibn Ziyad's armies cross at Gibraltar and shatter the Visigothic kingdom at Guadalete, bringing nearly all of Christian Iberia under the Caliphate.

source: Willibald, Vita Bonifatii; the Letters of Boniface
notes: In the forests of Hesse the English monk Boniface fells the sacred Oak of Thor unharmed, winning the Germans to Christ before his martyrdom in Frisia in 754.

source: Theophanes, Chronographia; John of Damascus, Three Treatises on the Divine Images
notes: Emperor Leo III orders the sacred images stripped from Byzantine churches, igniting a bitter century of iconoclasm that convulses the Eastern church.

source: Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (787), the Seventh Ecumenical Council
notes: The Seventh Ecumenical Council, gathered under Empress Irene, restores the veneration of icons, defining that the honor paid to the image passes to its prototype.

source: Einhard, Vita Karoli Magni; Royal Frankish Annals; Liber Pontificalis (Life of Leo III)
notes: On Christmas Day in St. Peter's, Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne 'Emperor of the Romans,' reviving a Western empire and deepening the rift with Byzantium.
In Constantinople the Empress Theodora restores the holy icons for good; the Orthodox still celebrate this 'Triumph of Orthodoxy' on the first Sunday of Lent.

source: Vita Constantini and Vita Methodii (Old Church Slavonic Lives of the brothers)
notes: The brothers Cyril and Methodius carry the gospel to the Slavs of Great Moravia, inventing an alphabet and translating the liturgy into the Slavonic tongue.

source: Photius, Encyclical to the Eastern Patriarchs (867); Mansi, Sacrorum Conciliorum Collectio
notes: Pope Nicholas I and Patriarch Photius of Constantinople hurl mutual condemnations over jurisdiction and the added Filioque, a bitter foretaste of 1054.

source: Responsa Nicolai ad consulta Bulgarorum (866); Theophanes Continuatus
notes: Khan Boris I of Bulgaria receives baptism from Byzantium, drawing his people into the Orthodox fold and its new Slavonic worship.

source: Russian Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let / Tale of Bygone Years)
notes: Prince Vladimir of Kiev is baptized and leads his people into the Dnieper, binding the Rus to Byzantine Orthodoxy and shaping the soul of Russia.

source: Accounts of Cardinal Humbert & Patriarch Michael Cerularius; Steven Runciman, The Eastern Schism (1955)
notes: Legates of Rome and the Patriarch of Constantinople excommunicate one another over papal authority and the added 'filioque' — and Christendom splits in two: Roman Catholic in the Latin West, Eastern Orthodox in the Greek East. The breach has never healed.

event: Gregory VII & the Humiliation at Canossa
source: Gregory VII, Dictatus Papae (1075); Lambert of Hersfeld, Annals
notes: Barefoot in the snow outside the Alpine castle of Canossa, Emperor Henry IV begs absolution for three days from Pope Gregory VII, who had asserted the Church's freedom from kings in the great Investiture struggle.

source: Anselm of Canterbury, Proslogion (c. 1077-78); later Cur Deus Homo (1098)
notes: At the abbey of Bec in Normandy, Anselm frames his proof of God as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived,' pioneering the scholastic quest of faith seeking understanding.

source: Chronicles of Cluny; the abbacy of Hugh the Great (r. 1049-1109)
notes: Under Abbot Hugh the Great, the Burgundian monastery of Cluny begins the largest church in Christendom and spreads its reforming, prayer-soaked discipline across hundreds of houses in Europe.

event: The First Crusade Proclaimed at Clermont
source: Fulcher of Chartres; Robert the Monk, Historia Hierosolymitana
notes: At Clermont in France, Pope Urban II summons armed pilgrims to rescue the Holy Land and beleaguered Byzantium, and the crowd roars back 'Deus vult!' — 'God wills it!'

source: Gesta Francorum; Raymond of Aguilers; Fulcher of Chartres
notes: After a scorching siege the First Crusaders scale Jerusalem's walls on 15 July and slaughter its people, planting the Latin Kingdom in the land where Christ had walked.

source: William of St Thierry, Vita Prima Bernardi; Bernard's letters and sermons
notes: From the stark new abbey of Clairvaux, the eloquent Bernard leads the austere Cistercians, counsels popes and kings, and becomes the conscience of twelfth-century Christendom.

source: Text of the Concordat of Worms (1122); confirmed by the First Lateran Council (1123)
notes: At Worms in Germany, pope and emperor strike the peace that ends the Investiture Controversy — bishops to receive their spiritual office from the Church and their lands from the crown.

event: Peter Lombard's Four Books of Sentences
source: Peter Lombard, Sententiae in IV libris distinctae (c. 1150-58)
notes: In Paris the theologian Peter Lombard arranges the teachings of Scripture and the Fathers into his Four Books of Sentences, the standard theology textbook of the medieval schools for centuries.

event: The Universities of Paris and Oxford
source: Charter of Philip II Augustus (1200); statutes of Paris (1215); H. Rashdall, The Universities of Europe in the Middle Ages
notes: Out of the cathedral schools of Paris and Oxford, masters and students band into the first universities, forging the workshops where scholastic theology and the liberal arts would flourish.

source: Geoffrey of Villehardouin; Niketas Choniates (Byzantine account)
notes: Diverted from Egypt, the Fourth Crusade turns its swords on Christian Constantinople, plundering the Orthodox capital and its relics — a betrayal that hardened the East-West schism for centuries.

source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima; the Regula bullata (1223); Dominic's Order of Preachers (1216)
notes: Renouncing his father's wealth in Assisi, Francis embraces Lady Poverty and wins papal blessing for his barefoot friars, as Dominic soon raises his own Order of Preachers — the mendicant renewal of the Church.

event: Innocent III & the Fourth Lateran Council
source: Canons of the Fourth Lateran Council (1215)
notes: The formidable Pope Innocent III gathers over a thousand prelates in Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council, defining transubstantiation and requiring yearly confession at the very zenith of papal power.
The Dominican 'Angelic Doctor' weds Aristotle to the Gospel in his monumental Summa Theologica, the crowning synthesis of medieval thought, left unfinished when he laid down his pen and died.

source: The Templar of Tyre (Cronaca del Templare di Tiro); chronicles of the fall of Acre
notes: Acre falls to the Mamluk armies, snuffing out the last Crusader foothold on the Levantine coast and ending nearly two centuries of Latin warfare for the Holy Land.

source: Bull Unam Sanctam (1302); the 'Outrage of Anagni' (1303)
notes: In the bull Unam Sanctam, Boniface VIII proclaims that submission to the Roman pontiff is necessary for salvation, but his defeat by France's king soon exposes the overreach and decline of the medieval papacy.

source: Petrarch's letters (the 'Babylonian Captivity' epithet); standard papal histories
notes: For nearly seventy years the popes abandon Rome for Avignon on the French frontier, a gilded 'Babylonian Captivity' that drained the papacy's prestige across Christendom.

source: Gregory Palamas, Triads in Defense of the Holy Hesychasts; the Synodal Tome of 1351 (Council of Blachernae)
notes: On Mount Athos and in Constantinople, the monk Gregory Palamas defends the hesychasts' silent prayer and their vision of God's uncreated light, and councils vindicate him — shaping the mystical soul of Orthodoxy.

source: Standard histories of the Western Schism (rival lines of Rome, Avignon, and later Pisa)
notes: Rival popes at Rome and Avignon — and later a third at Pisa — each claim Saint Peter's chair and excommunicate the others, tearing Western Christendom's allegiance apart for nearly forty years.

event: Wycliffe, the English Bible & the Lollards
source: The Wycliffite Bible (1382-1395); Wycliffe, De veritate sacrae scripturae
notes: At Oxford the 'Morning Star of the Reformation,' John Wycliffe assails papal wealth and oversees the first full English Bible, sending his poor Lollard preachers out with Scripture in the people's tongue.

source: Peter of Mladonovice, Relatio; records of the Council of Constance
notes: Lured to the Council of Constance under a broken safe-conduct, the Bohemian reformer Jan Hus is condemned and burned at the stake, singing to the end and kindling the Hussite revolt in his homeland.

event: The Council of Constance Ends the Schism
source: Acts of the Council of Constance (1414-1418)
notes: Meeting in the imperial city of Constance, the great council deposes the rival claimants and elects Martin V to reunite the Roman obedience, even as it condemns the reformers Wycliffe and Hus.

event: The Council of Florence & the Failed Reunion
source: Acts of the Council of Ferrara-Florence; the union bull Laetentur Caeli (1439); Mark of Ephesus's dissent
notes: Desperate for Western help against the Turks, Byzantine envoys sign reunion with Rome at Florence, but the people of Constantinople repudiate it — 'Better the Sultan's turban than the Cardinal's hat.'

source: Doukas; Kritoboulos; George Sphrantzes (eyewitness Byzantine chronicles)
notes: Sultan Mehmed II's great cannon breach the ancient Theodosian walls; the last emperor Constantine XI falls sword in hand, Hagia Sophia becomes a mosque, and the thousand-year Byzantine Empire is extinguished.
In the German city of Mainz, Johann Gutenberg prints the Latin Bible with movable type, a quiet revolution that would soon flood Europe with books and speed the coming Reformation.

source: Chronicles of Ivan III; Philotheus of Pskov, 'Third Rome' epistle (c. 1510)
notes: Grand Prince Ivan III of Moscow weds the last Byzantine emperor's niece and takes up the double-headed eagle, and within a generation Russian monks hail Moscow as the 'Third Rome,' heir of fallen Constantinople and guardian of Orthodoxy.

source: Savonarola's sermons; contemporary Florentine accounts of his execution (1498)
notes: The fiery Dominican Girolamo Savonarola, having ruled Florence and thundered against Renaissance corruption, is excommunicated, hanged, and burned in the Piazza della Signoria.

source: Luther, Disputatio pro declaratione virtutis indulgentiarum (1517); Bainton, Here I Stand (1950)
notes: On the eve of All Saints' in Wittenberg, a monk posts ninety-five protests against indulgences, and the printing press scatters the sparks across Germany within weeks.

event: Diet of Worms & Luther's German Bible
source: Acts of the Diet of Worms (1521); Bainton, Here I Stand (1950)
notes: Summoned before emperor and empire at Worms, Luther refuses to recant, then in hiding at the Wartburg he gives Germany the New Testament in its own tongue.
In Zurich's Grossmunster, Huldrych Zwingli preaches straight through the Scriptures and wins the city at public disputation, launching a distinct Swiss Reformation apart from Luther.

source: Chronicle of the Hutterian Brethren; G. H. Williams, The Radical Reformation (1962)
notes: In a Zurich home a handful of radicals rebaptize one another as adult believers, birthing the free church, and within two years Felix Manz is drowned in the Limmat for it.

source: 26 Henry VIII c.1 (1534); A. G. Dickens, The English Reformation (1964)
notes: When Rome would not annul his marriage, Henry VIII has Parliament name him Supreme Head of the Church in England, tearing the island church from the pope.

source: Calvin, Institutio Christianae Religionis (1536); McGrath, A Life of John Calvin (1990)
notes: A French refugee of twenty-six publishes the Institutes and is pressed to stay in Geneva, where he forges the city into a model of Reformed faith and discipline.

source: Bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae (1540); O'Malley, The First Jesuits (1993)
notes: A wounded Basque soldier turned pilgrim wins papal approval in Rome for the Society of Jesus, shock troops of the Counter-Reformation and missionaries to the ends of the earth.

source: Canons and Decrees of the Council of Trent; Jedin, History of the Council of Trent
notes: Meeting on and off for eighteen years in the Alpine town of Trent, Rome answers the Reformers, reaffirming its doctrine and reforming its clergy for four centuries to come.

event: Cranmer & the Book of Common Prayer
source: The Book of Common Prayer (1549); MacCulloch, Thomas Cranmer (1996)
notes: Thomas Cranmer gives England worship in its own tongue, his cadences shaping English-speaking piety long after he burns at Oxford for his faith in 1556.

source: Peace of Augsburg (1555); Brady, German Histories in the Age of Reformations (2009)
notes: At the imperial diet in Augsburg a weary Charles V concedes 'cuius regio, eius religio' — each prince may choose Lutheran or Catholic for his lands — the first legal truce between the confessions.

source: Scots Confession (1560); Knox, History of the Reformation in Scotland
notes: Thundering back from Geneva, John Knox leads Scotland's Parliament to abolish the pope and embrace the Reformed faith, founding the Presbyterian Kirk.

source: Contemporary accounts; Diefendorf, Beneath the Cross (1991)
notes: On St. Bartholomew's Day the streets of Paris run with Huguenot blood as thousands of French Protestants are slaughtered, the wedding-week massacre spreading to the provinces.

event: The Russian Patriarchate & Moscow the Third Rome
source: Acts establishing the Moscow Patriarchate (1589); Ware, The Orthodox Church (rev. ed.)
notes: With Constantinople fallen to the Turk, the Metropolitan of Moscow is raised to Patriarch, and Russia takes up its calling as the 'Third Rome,' guardian of Orthodoxy for the East.

source: Smyth's writings; McBeth, The Baptist Heritage (1987)
notes: Among English exiles in Amsterdam, John Smyth baptizes himself and his flock on profession of faith, and the first Baptist congregation is born.

event: Thirty Years' War & Peace of Westphalia
source: Treaties of Westphalia (1648); C. V. Wedgwood, The Thirty Years War (1938)
notes: Ignited by a defenestration in Prague, the war bleeds central Europe until the Peace of Westphalia lets each land keep its own faith and ends the age of religious wars.
Fleeing to the New World, a band of Separatist Congregationalists lands at Plymouth and covenants together, planting self-governing Puritan churches on New England soil.

source: Fox, Journal; Braithwaite, The Beginnings of Quakerism (1912)
notes: On Firbank Fell George Fox preaches to a thousand seekers, gathering the Society of Friends, Quakers who trust the inner Light and refuse hat, oath, and sword.

source: Acts of the Moscow Councils of 1666-67; Crummey, The Old Believers and the World of Antichrist (1970)
notes: When Patriarch Nikon corrects the service books and the sign of the cross, Archpriest Avvakum and the Old Believers refuse, and the Russian church tears apart, thousands later burning rather than submit.

source: Edwards, A Faithful Narrative; Wesley, Journal; Noll, The Rise of Evangelicalism (2003)
notes: As Jonathan Edwards' Northampton revival and George Whitefield's open-air thunder sweep the colonies, John Wesley, his heart 'strangely warmed' in London the year before, takes to the fields and Methodism is born.

source: Carey, An Enquiry (1792); George, Faithful Witness (1991)
notes: A Northampton cobbler who cried 'Expect great things; attempt great things,' William Carey sails for India and opens the modern age of Protestant missions.

source: Cane Ridge revival accounts; Hatch, The Democratization of American Christianity (1989)
notes: At Cane Ridge on the Kentucky frontier, thousands fall under conviction in a week-long camp meeting, igniting the revival that would reshape American Christianity.

source: Judson's letters; Courtney Anderson, To the Golden Shore (1956)
notes: Adoniram and Ann Judson, among America's first foreign missionaries, reach Burma and labor years amid prison and grief before their first convert believes.

source: The Book of Mormon (1830); Bushman, Joseph Smith: Rough Stone Rolling (2005)
notes: In upstate New York the young Joseph Smith publishes the Book of Mormon and organizes the Latter-day Saints, a new American religion reaching beyond the Protestant fold.

source: Stone-Campbell union records; Declaration and Address (1809)
notes: On the Kentucky frontier Alexander Campbell and Barton Stone unite their movements, calling for 'no creed but Christ' and forming the Disciples and Churches of Christ.

source: Livingstone, Missionary Travels and Researches in South Africa (1857)
notes: David Livingstone plunges into unmapped Africa as missionary and explorer, his lonely treks against the slave trade stirring a continent's evangelization.

source: Palmer, The Way of Holiness (1843); Dieter, The Holiness Revival of the Nineteenth Century (1980)
notes: In New York parlors Phoebe Palmer teaches her 'altar theology' of entire sanctification, and the Holiness movement she mothers spreads through camp meetings across the Atlantic.

source: SDA General Conference records (1863); Knight, A Brief History of Seventh-day Adventists (1999)
notes: Guided by the visions of Ellen G. White, Sabbath-keeping believers organize at Battle Creek as the Seventh-day Adventist Church, awaiting Christ's soon return.

event: Hudson Taylor & the China Inland Mission
source: Taylor, China's Spiritual Need and Claims; Broomhall, Hudson Taylor and China's Open Century
notes: Wearing Chinese dress and trusting God for every need, Hudson Taylor founds the China Inland Mission to carry the gospel into China's unreached interior.

source: The Apostolic Faith newspaper (1906); Robeck, The Azusa Street Mission and Revival (2006)
notes: In a former stable on Azusa Street in Los Angeles, the black preacher William Seymour leads a revival of tongues and fire that births worldwide Pentecostalism.

event: Assemblies of God & the Foursquare Gospel
source: 1914 Hot Springs founding minutes; Blumhofer, Restoring the Faith (1993)
notes: Pentecostals gather at Hot Springs to form the Assemblies of God, and soon Aimee Semple McPherson's Angelus Temple and Foursquare Gospel carry the movement to radio and the masses.

source: The Fundamentals (1910-1915); Marsden, Fundamentalism and American Culture (1980)
notes: As modernist theology and Darwin's evolution divide the churches, the Scopes trial in Dayton pits fundamentalists against the age and denominations split over the Bible's authority.

event: The New Martyrs under Soviet Communism
source: Pospielovsky, The Russian Church under the Soviet Regime (1984)
notes: Under Stalin's Great Terror the Russian Orthodox Church is nearly annihilated, bishops shot and monasteries razed, yet the New Martyrs' witness endures beneath the atheist state.

source: Graham, Just As I Am; Wacker, America's Pastor (2014)
notes: A young evangelist's tent crusade in Los Angeles stretches to eight weeks and national fame, launching Billy Graham to preach to more people than anyone in history.

source: Documents of Vatican II (Lumen Gentium et al.); O'Malley, What Happened at Vatican II (2008)
notes: Pope John XXIII throws open the windows of the Church, and the council in Rome renews Catholic worship, welcomes the vernacular Mass, and reaches out to a modern world.

event: The Revival of Orthodoxy after Communism
source: Post-Soviet church reports; Ware, The Orthodox Church (rev. ed.)
notes: As the Soviet Union collapses, churches reopen across Russia and eastern Europe, and Orthodoxy rises from the catacombs to rebuild after seventy years of atheism.

source: Johnson & Zurlo, World Christian Encyclopedia (3rd ed., 2020); Jenkins, The Next Christendom (2002)
notes: A faith once centered in Europe now beats strongest in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, over two billion strong, even as the secular West empties its pews.

Constantius II convenes Constantinople and adopts the Homoian creed — the Son is simply 'like' the Father, with 'substance' language forbidden. For a time this, not Nicaea, is the empire's official faith.
Back from exile, Athanasius gathers a council at Alexandria to reconcile the divided Nicene parties, agreeing that 'one hypostasis' and 'three hypostases' need not divide the churches.
A regional synod in Phrygia issues sixty canons on worship and order and lists the books to be read as Scripture — an early witness to the forming New-Testament canon (it omits Revelation).

event: The Filioque Divides East and West
notes: Rome finally adds 'and the Son' (filioque) to the Creed that no ecumenical council authorized; the Greek East, which never accepts it, sees Rome altering the faith of the fathers — the doctrinal wedge that will split the Church.

The Seljuk Turks shatter the Byzantine army at Manzikert and flood into Anatolia — the Christian heartland of Asia Minor — beginning the long Byzantine decline that will end at Constantinople's walls, and spurring the West to launch the Crusades.
In Anatolia the Turkish frontier chief Osman founds the dynasty that will devour the Byzantine remnant, seize Constantinople, and rule the Christian East for six centuries.

event: The Ottomans Turned Back at Vienna
source: Contemporary accounts of the Siege of Vienna
notes: At the walls of Vienna the Ottoman advance into the heart of Europe crests and breaks — the high-water mark of Islam's centuries-long push against Latin Christendom.
